intuition: Visit the tree one level at a time using a queue. At the start of a level, count the nodes already in the queue. Process exactly that many nodes, adding their children for the next level. This keeps children out of their parents' output group.

Use a FIFO queue of nodes. Popping a parent and appending its children advances the frontier. The subtle issue is that the queue changes while a level is processed. Freeze its initial length so children added during this iteration wait for the next group instead of entering the current one.

Left-to-right order also follows from the queue discipline. Parents are removed in their existing left-to-right order, and each appends its left child before its right child. Thus the next frontier has the same desired ordering. A deque keeps removals constant time, unlike removing index zero from a Python list.

steps: For root [3,9,20,null,null,15,7], begin with queue=[3] and no completed levels.
Freeze size=1. Remove 3, collect [3], and append children 9 then 20. Save the first level.
Now freeze size=2. Remove 9, which has no children, then 20, whose children 15 and 7 join the queue.
The collected second level is [9,20]; newly queued children were excluded from its two removals.
Process the final queue [15,7] as one level. With no children left, return [[3],[9,20],[15,7]].

codeNotes.note: This snapshot is the current level’s boundary. Rechecking a growing queue length would mix child nodes into their parents’ group.
FIFO removal processes earlier, shallower discoveries first, and deque avoids the element-shifting cost of list.pop(0).
Append only after exactly size nodes have been processed, so every output list corresponds to one complete depth frontier.

keyDecision: Freeze the queue size before processing a level. New children belong to the next level.
